content: Early identification of asymptomatic children exposed to or infected with HIV is critical, and immunization programs provide an opportunity to integrate HIV testing at key points during the first two years of life. For example, HIV testing can coincide with the administration of the first dose of pentavalent and other vaccines at six weeks, the first dose of the measles vaccine at nine months, and the second dose of the measles vaccine at 18 months. This integration aligns with WHO recommendations and can enhance early infant diagnosis (EID) efforts. In addition to routine immunization schedules, outreach immunization sessions, supplemental immunization campaigns, and immunization coverage surveys can serve as platforms for other interventions, such as co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Co-trimoxazole is a medication used to prevent pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV-infected children. However, infants who are HIV-positive or have an unknown HIV status with symptoms consistent with HIV should not receive the BCG vaccine unless they are stable on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and show evidence of immunological recovery. WHO strongly recommends that all infants with unknown or uncertain HIV exposure seen at healthcare facilities around birth, during the first postnatal visit (usually at 4–6 weeks), or during other child health visits have their HIV exposure status determined. HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or as soon as possible thereafter. If an infant has an initial positive virological test result, ART should be initiated immediately without delay, even as a second specimen is collected to confirm the result. Delaying ART initiation while awaiting confirmatory test results can be life-threatening. Infants with signs or symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo serological testing, and if the result is positive, virological testing should follow. HIV-exposed infants should also undergo serological testing at around nine months of age. If the serological assay is reactive, a virological test should be performed to identify HIV-infected infants who require ART. For children aged 18 months or older with suspected HIV infection or exposure, standard diagnostic HIV serological testing algorithms used in adults should be applied. Studies have shown high acceptance rates (90–100%) among mothers for HIV testing of their infants during immunization visits, particularly during the first pentavalent or DTP vaccination visit. Integrated services have been reported to save time and costs, increase demand for HIV testing, and provide opportunities for mothers to learn their child’s HIV status and access treatment if needed. However, challenges include confidentiality concerns, perceived mandatory testing, increased workloads for healthcare workers, and community stigma, particularly in rural areas. Stigma associated with HIV testing may negatively impact the uptake of both HIV testing and vaccinations. Male circumcision has been shown to reduce the risk of heterosexually acquired HIV infection in men by approximately 60%. Since 2007, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) programs have been implemented in 14 priority countries in East and Southern Africa. These programs have successfully reduced HIV incidence in communities. However, cases of tetanus have been reported following circumcision, particularly with device-based methods or inappropriate wound care practices. To mitigate tetanus risk, WHO recommends that individuals undergoing circumcision be adequately protected through tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) immunization. WHO advises a three-dose TTCV primary series, starting as early as six weeks of age, with subsequent doses given at least four weeks apart and completed by six months of age. Three booster doses should be administered at 12–23 months, 4–7 years, and 9–15 years of age, with at least four years between booster doses. For circumcision using device methods, two TTCV doses at least four weeks apart, with the second dose administered at least two weeks before device placement, are recommended. Alternatively, a single booster dose may be given if the individual has previously received three infant doses or one dose during adolescence or adulthood. Clean care practices, including proper skin preparation and personal hygiene, are essential to minimize infection risks during and after circumcision procedures.
